definition: A statement or situation that seems to contradict itself but may still be true.
example: It is a paradox that the busiest people often seem to find the most time to help others.
nuance: A contradiction is simply inconsistent, but a paradox only seems impossible and often hides a real truth.
prompt: A coach notices that her team plays better in weeks when it practices less.
options: The coach puzzled over the paradox that resting more made her players faster.
The coach introduced a new paradox for how drills would be scheduled each week.
It was a paradox that the players who trained hardest grew strongest.
The players performed a funny paradox of the coach's pep talk for the bus ride.
reasons: Doing less and improving more seems impossible yet turns out true, which is exactly a paradox.
This confuses the word with paradigm; a training model or plan is not a seeming contradiction.
Hard work leading to strength is what anyone would expect, so nothing here seems contradictory.
This mixes the word up with parody; a comic imitation is not a self-contradiction.

practice.prompt: A beginner learns that cutting back a rosebush makes it bloom more.
options: The gardener's prize rose was a paradox of beauty, admired by every judge.
The gardener solved the paradox by finding his lost trowel in the shed.
Pruning a plant to help it grow seemed like a paradox to the new gardener.
The gardener watered the roses every day, a paradox that kept them healthy.
reasons: This treats the word like paragon; a perfect example of beauty contains no contradiction.
A misplaced tool is just a mystery, not an idea that seems to argue against itself.
Removing parts of a plant so it flourishes sounds self-defeating but works, so the word fits.
Water keeping plants healthy is ordinary cause and effect, with no apparent conflict.
